newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli CPI-linked bonds close higher.
newsitem.headline: Israeli CPI-linked bonds close higher.

text.p: Israeli CPI-linked bonds closed higher on Sunday in very quiet trading ahead of the Bank of Israel announcement on Febuary interest rates on Monday, traders said.
* Unlinked government bonds (Gilon -- issued for four years): +0.01 pct to 101.83
* Bank of Israel short-term Makam bills: +0.09 pct to 101.15.
Volume was very low at 97 million shekels.
"Prices continue to rise but investors are showing little interest in bonds and the market is very quiet," said a trader at Bank Hapoalim.
"Investors expect only a moderate rate cut of 0.5 percentage points or less, but the central bank might also leave it unchanged," said Uri Schur at Eyal Securities.

Nevertheless Roy Meir of Simodan said he believed the long-range outlook for interest rates was good. "The Bank of Israel is expected to lower its key interest rate by only 0.3 to 0.5 points," he said. "But even if it leaves it unchanged it is clear that in the long run the central bank has to lower its key lending rate."
Inflation-linked bonds continued to rise today, which Meir attributed to a supply-demand imbalance.

"Mutual funds have to buy these bonds, but the central bank stopped issuing them and so prices are rising," Meir said. "This led to a further decline in yields on long-bonds, which fell today to only 4.3 percent."
Yields on unlinked bonds have fallen to 14.3 percent from 14.8 percent over the last month, which Meir said reflects expectations for a rate cut of 0.5 percentage points.

Other traders attributed the rise in unlinked bonds to expectations for declining inflation. "Unlinked bonds and Makams are still attractive for investors who predict annual inflation of only nine percent," the Hapoalim trader said.
Traders said dollar-linked bonds closed slightly lower in mixed trade in response to the decline of the U.S. currency on Friday.
Note: Makams are zero-coupon unlinked certificates with durations of three months to one year. The Bank of Israel issues Makams to absorb liquidity.
